transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Whenever we’re supposed to sit and do quiet activities here, I just can’t seem to keep myself still and focused on them. My daughter actually suggested I get evaluated because I recently moved into a senior living complex, and we wanted to make sure the staff doesn't mistake my restlessness for agitation or memory problems.
Have you struggled with this restlessness and difficulty focusing since you were a child, or is this a relatively new change that has developed recently?

It’s actually a lifelong thing; even back in grade school, my teachers were always telling me to stay in my seat, and my mother said I was always "on the go." But it has become much more of a problem recently, especially since I moved into this senior complex about a year and a half ago with all of its structured schedules.
Besides your restlessness, have you noticed any significant recent changes in your memory, such as difficulty finding words, forgetting familiar names, or losing track of your daily routine?

Oh, no, not at all—my mind and memory feel completely fine, and I don't have any trouble finding words or names. My daughter only wanted me to get this evaluation because she was worried the staff might mistake my physical restlessness for agitation or early cognitive decline.
Besides being restless, do you often find yourself interrupting others in conversation, making impulsive decisions, or losing track of your belongings because you are easily distracted?

Yes, I definitely struggle with interrupting—during our resident meetings, I tend to jump in and finish people's sentences or blurt out answers before they're done, which has been quite embarrassing. However, I don't really have any issues with losing track of my belongings or making big impulsive decisions.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a lifelong pattern of persistent inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity that began in childhood and continues to cause functional impairment in her current living environment. Cognitive decline (dementia) was ruled out as the cause of her restlessness.
